text: Applying DNA barcoding to conservation practice: a case study of endangered birds and large mammals in China

Owning to advantages over traditional species identification methods, DNA barcoding is suggested to be a promising tool in conservation research. However, the use of DNA barcoding to accurately identify unknown samples in conservation practices has not been well documented in the literature. To illustrate this issue, we implemented a survey of endangered birds and mammals in China based on mitochondrial Cytochrome c Oxidase subunit I (COI) gene. We included mostly confiscated specimens and non-invasive samples while concealing species information to simulate real-world scenarios of identification. In total, 47 avian and 39 mammalian specimen were re-identified by sequential analyses of online species assignment, genetic distances, phylogenetic reconstruction, and diagnostic nucleotide method. With this multiple analyses approach, 82 individuals were accurately assigned to the species level and four individuals to the genus level. 78.72% of the avian specimen and 87.18% of mammalian specimen identifications were consistent with morphological classification. Among those inconsistent with morphological classification, we Communicated by Anurag chaurasia.

Considered a biodiversity hotspot, southwest China hosts a large number of birds and mammals (Myers et al. 2000;Schipper et al. 2008), most of which are endemic and categorized as threatened or endangered species on the IUCN red list (www.iucnredlist. org). Despite legal protection, many species still suffer from poaching and overexploitation (Yiming and Wilcove 2005;Zhang et al. 2008). This pressure stems from the high demand for birds or mammals that are considered to have ornamental value or applications in Chinese medicine, such as the tiger (bone), bear (gallbladder), and forest musk deer (musk) (Feng et al. 2009;Lau et al. 2010;Li and Zhu 2014;Zhou et al. 2004). Rapid and accurate species identification is crucial for conservation management to prohibit the overexploitation and poaching of protected species. While traditional morphological identification practices are often difficult to apply to conservation research due to the scarcity of in-tact specimens, the accurate identification of specimens is essential for administrative officials to justly prosecute violators of endangered species protection laws and thus warrants the need for accurate and efficient molecular methods of species identification.
DNA barcoding has proven to be a powerful tool for rapid species assignment and cryptic species discovery, with promising applications in animal conservation (Hebert et al. 2003(Hebert et al. , 2004a;;Kress et al. 2015;Vernooy et al. 2010). DNA barcoding requires only a trace of DNA for species identification, permitting the use of damaged or incomplete specimens. Furthermore, this molecular procedure is relatively simpler and much faster than that of traditional morphological methods concerning taxonomy, i.e. the identification of new species, thereby accelerating the species identification process (Hebert and Gregory 2005). DNA barcoding also allows those researchers lacking expertise in morphological taxonomy to carry out accurate assessments of unknown specimens (Hebert and Gregory 2005). In last two decades, DNA barcoding of animals has been extensively tested and has gained considerable validation in species authentication of many taxa, including plankton, insects, fishes, birds and mammals (Borisenko et al. 2008;Hajibabaei et al. 2006;Hebert et al. 2004b;Hubert et al. 2008;Nagy et al. 2012;Oba et al. 2015). As a result of recent efforts, researchers have developed a relatively comprehensive reference database of DNA barcodes-laying a solid foundation for the application of DNA barcoding to conservation.
Despite the wide applicability of DNA barcoding in many taxa, the use of DNA barcoding for the identification of unknown specimens in real-world conditions has not been extensively surveyed. Previous DNA barcoding studies have heavily relied on invasive tissue samples, most of which having employed one or two analytical methods for species identification in biodiversity conservation (Ardura et al. 2010;Gonc ¸alves et al. 2015), food traceability (Quinto et al. 2016;Wong andHanner 2008), diet analyses (Co ˆte ´et al. 2013;Jo et al. 2015), bird strikes (Dove et al. 2008;Waugh et al. 2011) and biosecurity etc. (Armstrong and Ball 2005;Gonza ´lez-Varo et al. 2014). There are, however, inherent limitations and complementary advantages in these DNA barcoding analyses (DeSalle et al. 2005;van Velzen et al. 2012). It is wise to use multiple analytical methods to get high accuracy in DNA barcoding identification in conservation practices.
Here, we aimed to illustrate how to efficiently employ DNA barcoding for the identification of unknown specimens in practical conservation work, with a case study of many key protected birds and big mammals in China. Multiple DNA barcoding analytic approaches were chosen to achieve high species identification resolution step by step. This case study not only enhances the biotic barcode database, but also provides a guide for the application of DNA barcoding to the identification of unknown samples in conservation practice.

A total of 94 inventory samples were included (Online Resource Table 1). To mimic authentic conservation scenarios, we focused on confiscated specimens (fur and fragmented or corrupted tissues) and non-invasive samples (feather, fur and faeces). Some blood samples were collected via physical examination. Tissue and faeces samples were stored at -20 °C in 95% ethanol (24 ? 3 individuals). Fifty-six blood samples were stored at -20 °C with anticoagulant. Feather (four individuals) and fur samples (seven individuals) were freeze-dried. All samples were empirically identified based on morphological characters by experts from the Nature Museum at Sichuan University, representing 22 species of bird (15 genera, 7 families) and 22 species of mammals (17 genera, 9 families) (MacKinnon et al. 2000;Smith et al. 2010).
These samples represent endangered or rare species that are of great importance to the conservation of biodiversity in China, including 17 species of first-grade, state-protected animals, such as Sichuan Partridge (Arborophila rufipectus), black-necked crane (Grus nigricollis), south China tiger (Panthera tigris amoyensis) and sika deer (Cervus nippon), as well as 15 species of second-grade, state-protected animals, such as white-naped crane (Grus vipio) and blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur). Many of the represented species are also recognized internationally as vulnerable (V), endangered (E) or critically endangered (CE) by the IUCN Red List (version 2015-4).
To simulate real-world scenarios, we concealed species information, using only catalogue numbers to label specimens.
All samples were obtained in accordance with Chinese regulations for the implementation of protection of terrestrial wild animals (State Council Decree [1992] No. 13). All protocols were approved by the Guidelines for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the Ethics Committee of Sichuan University (Chengdu, China).

Genomic DNA was extracted using a standard proteinase K/phenol method with minor modifications (Sambrook and Russell 2001). Fecal DNA extractions were performed using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen Inc) under the manufacturer's instructions. DNA quality was verified by 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis. An approximately 650 bp region near the 5 0 terminus of the COI gene was amplified as described in Li et al. (2015). For amplification, we employed the universal primers for birds (BirdF1, FalcoFa, BirdR1 and BirdR2) (Kerr et al. 2007) and vertebrates (VF1/VR1 and VF1d/VR1d) (Ivanova et al. 2006;Ward et al. 2005) and designed primers GF_1/GR_1 for Gruidae to maximize amplicon recovery. All primers are listed in Online Resource Table 2.
Amplicons were purified using a DNA gel extraction kit (OMEGA) and bidirectionally sequenced by Invitrogen Trading Guangzhou Co. Ltd. The contigs were assembled with CExpress 9.1, aligned and trimmed to 648 bp after manual examination in MEGA 5.2 (Tamura et al. 2011) and translated into amino acids sequences, to verify that they were free of stop codons and gaps in case of pseudogenes. These COI sequences were submitted to GenBank (Accession Numbers KJ862125-KJ862210).

Sequences were first run through an online nucleotide BLAST (http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov/Blast.cgi) with the parameter ''program selection'' set at ''highly similar sequences''. The most similar sequence (called ''best hit'') with the highest similarity was obtained based upon pairwise alignments by querying individual COI sequences against the nucleotide database. Hits were filtered to those with both coverages and similarities greater than 95%. Queries were then assigned to the species associated with its best hit(s). If there was no such best hit or best hits contained more than one species, the assignment of queries could not be determined. Taking GenBank sequences into account, best hits should exclude the query sequence itself.
Meanwhile, the online BOLD identification system (IDS) was employed to assign the queries (http://www.barcodinglife.com/index.php/IDS_OpenIdEngine) (Ratnasingham and Hebert 2013). We chose ''Animal Identification [COI]'' database and searched ''Species Level Barcode Records'', then input the query sequences in fasta format. This procedure assigns the queries to species or genus level in most cases, showing the most likely candidate species along with top 20 matches while providing tree-based identification. We referred to the trees to infer the taxonomy when the queries were ambiguously identified.
We retrieved conspecific and congeneric COI sequences (Online Resource Table 3) from GenBank according to the preliminary identifications of online analyses, and conducted the following analyses to further discriminate species of the queries.
Kimura two-parameter (K2P) (Kimura 1980) pairwise distances were calculated for birds and mammals in MEGA5.2 (Tamura et al. 2011). Nucleotide gaps were treated as pairwise deletions. Uniform substitution rate was used with substitutions including both transitions and transversions. Genetic distances were calculated at three levels separately: within species, genera and families based on the online identifications, mainly following taxonomic organization suggested by MacKinnon et al. (2000) and Smith et al. (2010). The samples with genetic distances close to the average genetic divergence and interspecific distances generally being greater than their intraspecific distances are considered to be accurately identified, while the specimens with extremely large conspecific genetic distances or very small congeneric distances, for example zero, are thought to be misidentified, although extremely small congeneric distances could reflect real biological phenomena, such as incomplete lineage sorting, hybridization or recent speciation.
Phylogenetic trees were constructed assuming that samples of distinct species would form discrete clusters in a DNA barcode tree. Neighbour joining trees (Saitou and Nei 1987) based on K2P distances of the two datasets were implemented separately in MEGA5.2 (Tamura et al. 2011). We used 1000 bootstrap replicates to assess branch support. Other parameters were set the same as calculating K2P pairwise distances. Typical of DNA barcoding studies, we mainly focused on whether individuals of the same species were clustered together, rather than on the evolutionary relationships between species. We employed the strict tree-based criterion that queries are assigned to the taxon comprising of conspecific members, in which they are nested (Wilson et al. 2011).
To test the robustness of our results and clarify ambiguous identifications, we carried out diagnostic character-based identification with program BLOG2.0 (Weitschek et al. 2013). Two files in fasta format were prepared: one file consisted of a training set of sequences with species assignments and the other contained a testing set of sequences without species information. Classification logic formulas were created from the training set to identify the testing set. The queries were treated so as to maximize the percentage of testing sequences. Parameters for feature selection were set as described in Li et al. (2015). The logic formula with the lowest false positive rate was used for identification. To improve the reliability of the outputs we discarded the GenBank sequences with extremely large intraspecific distances or those failing to cluster with congeneric sequences.

In total, 47 individual birds and 39 individual mammals were successfully sequenced for molecular identification. Three bird sequences and five feline sequences (underlined in Online Resource Table 1) were found to be pseudogenes due to indels and stop codons, then were discarded in subsequent analyses. The amplification rates were 94% for birds and 88.64% for mammals respectively, suggesting strong primer performance.

Forty-three avian specimens were identified down to the species level by online BLAST with an effective identification rate of 91.49%. Identification failed for four specimens (see Online Resource Table 4) either because the best hits contained sequences of different species (B03), or because of the low identity of 90% (N9, N10 and N11). However, among the 43 assignments, there were six ambiguous identifications (N1, N2, N17, N23, N24 and N25, Online Resource Table 4a). This ambiguity arose from best hits with identity of 99% representing several closely related species.
Mammalian specimens experienced a 100% effective identification rate, with individuals identified down to species for all specimens. However, the classification of five individuals S29, S30, S36, and S61 (Online Resource Table 4b) was unreliable due to reasons described above regarding the ambiguity of avian specimens.

The effective identification rate of online IDS analyses was 95.74% for birds. Among the 45 successful assignments, 31 were assigned to the species level and 14 were classified to genus. The identification of two samples (B10 and B33) failed due to the absence of closely related DNA barcodes in the database (denoted by ''no match''). For mammalian specimens, 97.44% of queries were successfully classified by online IDS, 24 of which were classified to the species level and 14 of which were classified to the genus level. As above, failure to identify one individual (S49) was a result of ''no match'' in the DNA barcode database.
According to the preliminary identifications, we downloaded COI sequences of related species to conduct the following analyses, including 189 individuals representing 78 avian species and 147 individuals representing 63 mammalian species (Online Resource Table 3). About 64% of avian species and 56% of mammalian species were represented by more than two individuals in the combined dataset.

K2P pairwise distances of the birds and mammals are summarized in Table 1. Overall, the genetic distances increased as the taxonomic level climbed for both datasets, with true barcode gaps (Meier et al. 2006) being present only in Gruidae, Ciconiidae and Lorisidae. The average K2P pairwise distances of birds within species and genera were 0.40 and 7.64%, respectively. That is, the mean congeneric distance of birds was approximately 19 times the mean conspecific distance. The average intraspecific distance of mammalian specimens was 1.10% with an average interspecific distance of 6.07%, which showed that the average intraspecific genetic divergence of mammals was larger than that of birds, and the gap between the average interspecific and intraspecific genetic distance was generally narrower than that of birds. The italic values stand for genetic distances of taxonomic groups with barcoding gaps
Those individuals with overlapping conspecific and congeneric genetic distances (Online Resource Table 5) included three scenarios. First, the individuals had large intraspecific distances (Online Resource Table 5a), most of them only successfully identified as a result of much larger interspecific distances to other samples. The queries with intraspecific distances being generally greater than their interspecific distances were unidentified, including S14, S15, and S18. The downloaded sequence NC016666 labelled as Cebus apella in GenBank had an extremely large intraspecific distance of 31.45%, which must be mislabelled, and was removed from the database in the following analyses. Second, the individuals had unexpectedly low interspecific distances (Online Resource Table 5b) and third, the individuals of different species shared the same DNA barcodes with an interspecific distance of zero (Table 2), which failed to be identified here.

The NJ trees of birds and mammals are showed in Online Resource Figs. 1 and2, respectively. According to the strict identification criterion of Wilson et al. (2011), 38 out of 47 avian specimens were successfully assigned to species level based on clustered nests containing conspecific samples with bootstrap support values greater than 90%. Taking into account the individuals classified to the genus level (B03, N12, N13 and N14), the efficient identification rate of birds was 89.36%. Specimen B03, belonging to a cluster containing Accipiter virgatus and A. gularis, shared the same DNA barcode with both species. N12, N13 and N14 formed a sister clade to Mycteria leucocephala then clustered with M. Americana, and therefore, were assigned to the genus Mycteria (Fig. 1). Lacking conspecific DNA barcodes, five specimens (B08, B15, N9, N10 and N11) were only classified to family level. N9, N10 and N11 paralleled to Mycteria and nested into a cohesive clade of Ciconiidae (Fig. 1). Similarly, B08 and B15 were identified as Strigidae (Online Resource Fig. 1a).
Thirty-one mammal queries were successfully identified to the species level and five to genus by the DNA barcode tree (Online Resource Fig. 2), with an efficient identification rate of 92.31%. Five individuals (S29, S30, S36, S61 and S64) nested in a monospecific clade containing congeneric samples, respectively. Three samples (S14, S15 and S18) forming a clade with Panthera onca and then paralleling to Uncia uncia (synonym: P. uncia), could only be assigned to Felidae (Online Resource Fig. 2c).
In addition, most of the closely related species with small interspecific distances (Strix davidi and S. uralensis, Cervus elaphus and C. nippon) were successfully classified in the trees by forming distinct and cohesive clades. Meanwhile, some species with large intraspecific distances were also successfully identified by forming monospecific clades (A. gentilis, and Muntiacus reevesi). However, identification of several species with large intraspecific distances (C. elaphus, Elaphurus davidianus, Papio anubis, and Chlorocebus aethiops) failed due to their resolving into paraphyletic groups. Again, NJ trees could not discriminate samples sharing the same DNA barcode.

We conducted BLOG analysis with the combined data to validate our identification results. Most investigated species obtained classification logic formulas (Online Resource Table 6) supporting our previous species assignments. The failed identifications with no diagnostic formulas arose from species sharing DNA barcode, as shown in Table 2.

section: combining different dna barcoding identification results
text: DNA barcoding identifications based on different analytic methods are summarized in Table 3 and Online Resource Table 7, and compared with the morphologically putative classification. In summary, 82 out of 86 queries were effectively classified to species and four individuals to genus, and 19 queries were successfully classified after interpretation of results from multiple analyses. The DNA barcoding identifications were congruent with morphological classification in 78.72% birds and 87.18% mammals respectively. For the 15 cases which were incongruent (Table 3), we inferred that seven samples were probably misidentified based on morphological analysis as their sibling species. Two samples were most likely mislabelled as distantly-related species, and four individuals were only classified to genus based on shared DNA barcode (B03) or lacking conspecific barcodes (N12-N14). Individual S29 and S61, identified to species based on DNA barcoding while morphologically classified as 'Papio sp.', were also counted in the incongruent cases.

A successful application of DNA barcoding identification to conservation
Although DNA barcoding has been applied to a vast array of fauna, most of these studies mainly focused on whether DNA barcoding was suitable for species assignation of certain animal groups (Taylor and Harris 2012). The applications of DNA barcoding to identify unknown specimens in animal conservation practices have yet to be intensively studied.
Our research represents a case study of DNA barcoding application to conservation practices based on key protected bird and large mammal species in China, many of which are currently listed as threatened or endangered on the IUCN red list. To better illustrate the efficiency and reliability of barcoding identification in real-world scenarios of conservation, we mimicked the conditions by using real confiscated materials (fur and fragmented or corrupted tissues) or non-invasive samples (feather, faeces), and by concealing species information of samples prior to molecular identification. With multiple DNA barcoding analyses based on COI sequences, 82 out of 86 unknown samples were accurately identified to the species level and four samples to the genus level, most of which were concordant with morphological classifications. Moreover, some individuals, such as S29 and S61 that were only classified to genus level ('Papio sp.') through the morphological approach, were successfully identified to species through DNA barcodes. Our case study demonstrated the amenability and reliability of this molecular species identification tool in conservation practices.

section: multiple analyses generating reliable dna barcoding identification
text:
Incomplete or decayed samples of unknown specimens are often difficult or impossible to identify through traditional morphological classification procedures, making species identification one of the biggest challenges in conservation practices. The simple online DNA barcoding identification analysis based on the GenBank or BOLD databases has proven to be efficient and reliable in many studies (Barber and Boyce 2006;Co ˆte ´et al. 2013;Dalton and Kotze 2011) as well as in our research. However, there was generally no best-performing method i.e., a given method could perform better than another for a given taxonomic scenario, whereas the reverse could be true for another one, see also Austerlitz et al. (2009). To meet the high accuracy requirement in species assignation of unknown specimens in conservation practice, it is better to use a combined analytical approach to conduct DNA barcoding identification. In this case study, we first got a species framework through online BLAST and IDS analysis. Genetic distance and phylogenetic relationship were then assessed from a combination of sample sequences and public barcodes to get detailed information. Lastly, character-based analyses-BLOG was employed to verify the obtained results, especially for weak positive results. This approach proved effective. Totally, 95.35% unknown samples were accurately identified to species, and approximately 22% of which that failed to be identified by one method, were successfully classified through the combined analytical approach. Genetic distance and phylogenetic reconstruction were necessary complementary analyses to online identification analyses, given that they helped accurately identify the queries that got different species classification in the two online analyses (Table 3). For example, B10 and B33, unidentified in IDS, were successfully assigned by BLAST, genetic distance, NJ tree and BLOG. N12-N14 were ambiguously classified as M. leucocephala with weak support from online analyses, genetic distances and phylogenetic tree, while the BLOG analysis revealed that the diagnostic characters drawn from them (Pos66 = C, Pos399 = A, Pos444 = T, Pos627 = T) were incongruent with that from the downloaded sequences of M. leucocephala (HM804932 and HM804933, Pos30 = T, Pos207 = C, Pos399 = G, Pos627 = T), and there were 16 different nucleotide positions between them after realignment in MEGA 5.2 (Tamura et al. 2011), both indicating that N12-N14 belonged to a congeneric species of M. leucocephala. However, we need more information to clarify this issue.
Meanwhile, we have acknowledged the fact that discrepancies between BLAST and BOLD identification results are due to slight differences in the sequence libraries and that the similarity between the results of the various methods, especially BLAST and the three additional methods, is due to the fact that they are mainly based on the same sequences.

section: potential misidentifications and mislabelling in the inventory samples
text:
Misidentification and mislabelling of samples are not rare in the previous studies (Pleijel et al. 2008;Ward et al. 2009;Yang et al. 2014) resulting in potential errors and confusion in later research. DNA barcoding provides a robust method to recognize potential cases of morphological misidentifications and mislabelling in inventory samples. For instance, it is highly likely that B16 and S51 were mislabelled as distantly related species due to the fact that all analytical methods generated consistent and unambiguous species classification with strong statistical support. Additionally, seven samples were highly likely to be misidentified from previous morphological analysis, involving species that are prone to be misidentification due to subtle morphological differences among sister species.
For example, B05 (Falco rusticolus) was empirically misidentified as F. cherrug. The morphological identification of raptors is difficult even for experts due to ambiguous identification criterion as well as morphological variation within species relative to age, gender, season and geographical distribution (Gamauf et al. 1998;Pearlstine and Thompson 2004). Morphologically F. cherrug cannot be clearly defined and shares overlapping phenotypic characteristics with F. rusticolus especially (Eastham et al. 2001). Other misidentifications (N7, N8, N31, N32) occurred between Ciconia ciconia and C. boyciana for similar reasons related to morphology. We also found misidentifications in several of our mammalian specimens, including Trachypithecus hatinhensis (S63, as T. francoisi) and Nycticebus pygmaeus (S49, as N. coucang). Unfortunately, most of the incongruent samples were incomplete making it impossible to re-identify them by the morphological method.

section: factors impacting the application of dna barcoding to conservation practices
text:
To apply DNA barcoding to conservation and other practical or academic work as a routine method, we must acknowledge several factors. Sharing the same DNA barcode is the most notable issue, though it happens only occasionally. Employing multiple analytical methods will have minimal impact on improving applicability in this case. Factors contributing to this issue include incomplete lineage sorting and introgression. For instance, we failed to identify B03 because of its sharing barcode with A. virgatus and A. gularis. To address such ambiguities, we advise including as many closely related species as possible or trying another DNA barcode marker.
Special attention should be paid to sibling species for they tend to be similar in morphology and genetic background, such as reported in Dixon (2012), thus, tend to be misidentified either by morphological approaches or DNA barcoding. The fewer consistencies detected between DNA barcoding and morphological identification in birds (78.72%) than that in mammals (87.18%) likely resulted from the higher number of sibling species included in our avian dataset.
The reference database also plays an important role in the applicability of DNA barcoding identification. Generally involving more barcodes of more species would improve the species assignment performance (Dinca ˘et al. 2011). The identification failure of N12-N14 was mainly due to lacking DNA barcodes of M. ibis and other congeneric species. Meanwhile, the accurate information of downloaded barcodes is essential to obtain successful identification, including the species name and collection details. We found that the downloaded sequence NC016666 was labelled incorrect species information and similar cases had been mentioned in previous studies (Harris 2003;Mitchell 2008).

In this case study, DNA barcoding was applied to species identification in conservation practices based on endangered birds and large mammals in China. In order to better investigate the efficiency and feasibility of DNA barcoding identification in practical work, we used confiscated specimens and non-invasive samples and concealed species information during molecular identification. Forty-seven birds and 39 mammals were reidentified by DNA barcoding with sequential analyses of online primary species assignment, genetic distance, phylogenetic reconstruction, and diagnostic nucleotide methods. Eighty-two out of 86 queries were accurately assigned to a species level and four individuals to a genus level. Most of the DNA barcoding identifications (78.72% in birds and 87.18% in mammals) showed consistent species assignments with morphological classification. For those inconsistent with morphological classification, we identified seven potential morphological misidentifications and two cases of mislabelling with robust DNA barcoding evidence. The four samples identified to genus were mainly a result of sharing barcodes or lacking conspecific barcodes in the public database. Our survey showed a successful application of DNA barcoding to species authentication of unknown, incomplete samples in conservation practices and enriched the barcode database of endangered animals.

====================================================================================================
Evaluation of fecal DNA preservation and extraction methods in Przewalski's horse

The study compares the effects of three preservation methods (ethanol, drying and freezing) and two extraction methods (commercial kit and manual) on the PCR success rate and genotyping errors with fecal DNA from Przewalski's horse (Equus przewalskii). The interaction term between preservation and extraction was significant, and the highest amplification success rate (0.661) was obtained with samples stored in ethanol and extracted manually. The preservation method and time significantly impacted microsatellite amplification success rates. The method of preservation had an effect on the rate of allelic dropout (ADO), but the rate of false alleles (FA) varied nonsignificantly. Feces preserved in ethanol yielded the lowest ADO and FA, followed by drying and freezing. Our optimized preservation protocol probably have wide applicability to equids and rhinocerotids that produce large, high-fiber fecal pellets.

Noninvasive genetic sampling (NGS) has become indispensable tools for wildlife biologists. Technical improvements aim to reduce the genotyping error rates and thus generate more reliable conclusions (Bonin et al. 2004;Pompanon et al. 2005;Waits and Paetkau 2005). However, there is mounting concern that genotyping errors may bias the results and negatively influence the management of threatened and endangered species (Taberlet et al. 1999;Fernando et al. 2003;Hoffman and Amos 2005). Efficient fecal DNA preservation has proved to be essential in recovering high quantities of high quality DNA, which increase the success rate of PCR and reduce genotyping error rates (Wehausen et al. 2004;Piggott 2004;Nsubuga et al. 2004;Ha ´jkova ´et al. 2006). However, no universally effective and applicable preservation method has been developed, and methods can be inconsistently successful across different species and studies (Wasser et al. 1997;Murphy et al. 2000Murphy et al. , 2002;;Frantzen et al. 1998;Piggott and Taylor 2003;Panasci et al. 2011).
Starting in 1985, Przewalski's horses were reintroduced to China. However, genetic monitoring is still insufficient for the captive and released populations because of the difficulty of obtaining adequate DNA samples. Here we evaluate three fecal DNA preservation methods and two extraction methods for their suitability for the analysis of reintroduced Przewalski's horses.
Twenty fresh fecal samples were collected. Each fecal sample was divided into three parts, and each part was preserved using one of the following three methods. (1) Drying, (2) Ethanol, (3) Freezing. Fecal DNA extraction was carried out using TIANamp Stool DNA Kit (TIANGEN, Beijing) and the manual method (see supplementary file 1). Four horse-specific microsatellite loci (HTG08, CA425, HMS07, VHL20; Shiue et al. 1999) were examined. Each 25 lL PCR mixture contained 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 2.5 lL 109 buffer, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 0.4 lM of each primer pair, 0.2 lL 10 mg/mL BSA, 0.4 lL Taq polymerase (5U/lL, TaKaRa) and 2 lL fecal DNA. PCR conditions were as follows: 5 min at 95 °C followed by 35 cycles of 45 s at 95 °C, 1 min at the annealing temperature and 2 min at 72 °C, then 72 °C for 10 min. To optimize the combination of preservation and extraction methods, a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied to ranked data (Dytham 2011).
We evaluated the effects of preservation time (1 week, 2, 3, 6 and 9 months) on PCR success rates using Cochran test and McNemar's test. Preservation effectiveness was evaluated after 1 week, 2, 3 and 6 months of preservation time by calculating allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) using Wilcoxon's signed rank test (see experiment design in Table 1). Fecal genotypes were established by 8 % polyacrylamide gels based on the multiple-tubes approach (Taberlet et al. 1996). An allele was accepted only if it had been recorded at least twice (e.g. loci that gave rise to the same heterozygous genotype twice were accepted). In the ambiguous cases, a further four PCRs were performed to yield genotypes. Here, homozygote consensus genotypes were scored only if the same allele was documented all seven times. Samples for which genotypes could not be assigned after seven positive PCRs were classified as 'unknown'.
For the six trials of combined preservation and extraction methods, the preservation method had a significant effect on the PCR success rate (F (2,114) = 7.234, P = 0.027). Feces preserved with drying and freezing yielded lower PCR success rates than samples preserved with ethanol (Fig. 1). The interaction term between preservation and extraction was significant (F (2,114) = 22.111, P = 0.009). In comparison, the highest amplification success rate (0.661) was obtained with samples stored in ethanol and extracted with the manual method, and the lowest for the drying/kit method (0.367).
The preservation method had a significant effect on the microsatellite PCR success rate (v 4 2 = 44.31, P = 0.00). Time-dependent decay in PCR success rate was observed for samples stored under all three preservation methods (ethanol, v 4 2 = 11.652, P = 0.02; drying, v 4 2 = 12.696, P = 0.013; freezing, v 4 2 = 10.211, P = 0.037). For ethanol preservation, reduction was observed at 9 months relative to 1 week (P = 0.008) and 2 months (P = 0.025). The PCR success rate for samples preserved by drying was reduced significantly at 6 (P = 0.025) and 9 months (P = 0.014). Freezing also displayed a time-dependent reduction in PCR success rate over time, with significant reductions observed at 6 (P = 0.014) and 9 months (P = 0.020), and between 2 and 9 months (P = 0.034). Regardless of preservation time, the type of preservation affected the rate of ADO (v 5 2 = 12.338, P = 0.03), but the rate of FA varied nonsignificantly (v 5 2 = 10.725, P = 0.057). Feces preserved with ethanol yielded the lowest ADO and FA, followed by drying and freezing for the four preservation times (Fig. 2). Feces preserved with ethanol yielded no significant increase of ADO from 1 week to 6 months preservation time (P = 0.065). Our results suggest that our optimized method may be suitable for large ungulate mammals such as equids and rhinocerotids produce large, high-fiber fecal pellets.

Pros and cons of external swabbing of amphibians for genetic analyses

Non-invasive DNA sampling is an important tool in amphibian conservation. Buccal swabs are nowadays replacing the wounding toe-clipping method. Skin and cloaca swabbing are even less invasive and easier to handle than buccal swabbing, but could result in contaminations of genetic material. Therefore, we test if external skin and cloaca swabs are as reliable as buccal swabs for genetic analysis of amphibians. We analysed eight microsatellite loci for the common frog (Rana temporaria, Linnaeus 1758) and compared genotyping results for buccal, skin and cloaca swabs regarding allelic dropouts and false alleles. Furthermore, we compared two DNA extraction methods regarding efficiency and cost. DNA quality and quantity (amplification success, genotyping error rate, in nanogram per microlitre) were comparable among DNA sources and extraction methods. However, skin and cloaca samples exhibited high degrees of contamination with foreign individuals, which was due to sample collection during mating season. Here, we established a simple low budget procedure to receive DNA of amphibians avoiding stressful buccal swabbing or harmful toe clipping. However, the possibility of contaminations of external swabs has to be considered.

The global amphibian decline is a well-described problem. Stuart et al. (2004) showed that 43.2 % of amphibian species are experiencing some form of population decrease. Apart from climate change, over-exploitation of land and introduction of alien species, the main reasons for this decline are habitat loss and fragmentation (Stuart et al. 2004;Beebee and Griffiths 2005). For the protection of amphibian populations, information about their genetic structure is necessary to answer questions concerning population size, genetic diversity and gene flow among populations (Frankham et al. 2002). Toe clipping is a common method to collect genetic material of amphibians. However, it often leads to infections and reduction in mobility (McCarthy and Parris 2004). To avoid harmful injuries, the buccal swab method was established (Poschadel and Möller 2004), which is easy to perform, as cheap as other sampling procedures (Pidancier et al. 2003) and resulting in good DNA quality (Broquet et al. 2007). Moreover, storage and transport of swabs is uncomplicated (Poschadel and Möller 2004), and it is easier to get sampling permission for endangered species (Pidancier et al. 2003). In comparison to toe clipping, buccal swabbing is minimally invasive (Broquet et al. 2007). Nevertheless, opening the mouth of amphibians can be challenging and torturous, especially in small amphibians (e.g. newts). Prunier et al. (2012) already demonstrated the reliability of skin swabs compared to buccal swabs. However, contaminations of external swabs with DNA of foreign individuals are possible especially during mating season or when target species get in close contact during the sampling procedure. Therefore, we tested the reliability of skin and cloaca swabs compared to buccal swabs for genetic analysis of amphibians. Moreover, we compared the effectiveness of two differing DNA extraction methods for swab samples. marker availability. Samples were collected in Germany, Rhineland-Palatinate, near Ramstein-Miesenbach (49.27°N, 7.34°E) during mating season in March 2012. From 20 frogs, three swabs were taken each from buccal mucosa, skin and cloaca (N=60). We used sterile cotton swabs with a wooden handle and separate plastic cover (COPAN, Brescia, Italy). To take the buccal samples, the mouth was opened carefully with a flat plastic tip, and the swab was rolled over the inside of the cheek. For skin sampling, the cotton swab was rolled thoroughly over back, stomach and legs. For cloaca sample, the swab was rolled over the external cloaca. Samples were kept in a cooler box and stored at -23 °C.
Two DNA extraction methods were tested. Extractions of 44 samples (14 buccal, 15 skin, 15 cloaca) were conducted according to high salt DNA extraction protocol after Aljanabi and Martinez (1997) (ca. 0.10 €/sample). DNA of 16 samples (six buccal, five skin, five cloaca) was isolated using the Macherey Nagel NucleoSpin Tissue Kit (Düren, Germany; 2.18 €/sample) following the manufacturer's protocol. Nucleic acid concentrations were measured with NanoDrop ND-1000 Spectrophotometer (Peqlab, Erlangen, Germany).
We analysed eight variable microsatellite loci (Table 1; Matsuba and Merliä 2009) and amplified the fragments in two multiplex PCRs by using the QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Kit (Hilden, Germany). Primers were fluorescently labelled, and 10 pM of primer working solutions were mixed in two multiplex reactions in relation of 1 (Cy5):2 (Cy5.5):4 (Cy5.7). The PCR was conducted in 5 μL of final volume containing 2.5 μL QIAGEN Master Mix, 1.2 μL QIAGEN Solution, 0.3 μL Primer Mix and 1 μL DNA. PCR was conducted with Primus 96 Cycler (Peqlab Biotechnologie GmbH, Erlangen, Germany) with the following thermal profile: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 30 cycles of 30 s at 94 °C, 1.5 min at 55 °C and 1 min at 72 °C. A terminal elongation step was applied for 30 min at 60 °C. Amplification products were run on the CEQ 8000 Sequencer from Beckman Coulter (Krefeld, Germany). Buccal samples were repeated in a multi-tube approach (Taberlet et al. 1996) at least three times to identify real genotypes. Alleles had to be identical across at least two repetitions for heterozygotes and three repetitions for homozygotes (Hansen et al. 2008;Kolodziej et al. 2013). Skin and cloaca samples were repeated up to three times only in case of low amplification success or technical problems.
Fragments were analysed with the software GeneMarker 1.95 (SoftGenetics, State College, Pennsylvania). The genotypes of the buccal, skin and cloaca swabs of the same individual were compared for consistency, and allelic dropouts (ADO) as well as false alleles (FA) were counted. Genotyping error rates (GER) were calculated as the sum of ADO and FA for each buccal, skin and cloaca swabs per locus and across all loci. If skin or cloaca genotypes exhibited differing or additional alleles compared to the buccal genotype on at least two loci, we assigned this as a contamination with genetic material of additional individuals, which is also demonstrated by the high number of FAs found in skin and cloaca swabs which seem strongly correlated (Fig. 1).
Expected (H E ) and observed (H O ) heterozygosity were calculated with GENETIX 4.04 (http://kimura.univmontp2. fr/genetix/) based on buccal swab results. GER for extraction methods was calculated with buccal swab results as well. Percentage of genotyping success for each swabbing method was calculated over all loci and all repetitions. The raw data table of microsatellite alleles has been uploaded at the dryad database (http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/drayad.4qb53) and can be viewed under link (will be provided after acceptance for publication; excel spread sheet attached).

DNA quantity was comparable among both extraction methods. For the high salt extraction procedure, DNA concentrations ranged from 6.0 to 403.2 ng/μL (median=47.6 ng/μL; lower quartile=35.7 ng/μL; upper quartile=76.3 ng/μL). For the commercial kit, DNA concentration ranged from 18.0 to 303.3 ng/μL (median= 66.7 ng/μL; lower quartile =58.9 ng/μL; upper quartile =123.0 ng/μL). The high salt DNA extraction resulted in a GER of 0.3 %; for the commercial kit extraction, the GER was 0.9 % (Table 1). Thus, high salt extraction method is a reliable and cheap alternative to commercial kits. Nucleic acid concentration in DNA extracts of the different swabs ranged from 12.0 to 242.2 ng/μL (median=44.0; upper quartile=63.5; lower quartile=32.9) for buccal swabs; from 8.0 to 207.0 ng/μL (median=51.7; upper quartile=82.5; lower quartile=26.4) for skin swabs; and from 8.1 to 403.0 ng/μL (median=56.5; upper quartile=82.3; lower quartile=44.0) for cloaca swabs. This shows that extracted DNA quantity is comparable among the swab sources.
The genotyping success (GS), i.e. the amplification of each locus, was 71.8 % for buccal swabs, 41.4 % for skin swabs and 51.9 % for buccal swabs over all loci, which was mainly due to the non-amplification of one locus (BFG_099). Excluding BFG_099, the GS across the seven remaining loci resulted in 85.1, 62.1 and 72.2 %, respectively, which is well in the typical range for microsatellite studies using forensic samples (GS 20-70 %; Kolodziej et al. 2011). For the buccal swabs, the multi-tube approach resulted in a GER of only 0.4 % due to ADOs (Table 1). In comparison to other studies using forensic samples, this is a very low GER. Broquet (2004) showed an ADO rate of 11.3 % for faeces and 18.7 % for hair; in the study of Kolodziej et al. (2013) with faeces of wild boar, a GER of 4.3 % occurred. Although faeces and hair samples come along with more potential inhibition problems than buccal swabs, this comparison demonstrates that laboratory and scoring procedures were highly reliable in our study. Compared to the buccal swabs, the skin and cloaca swabs exhibited high GERs of 12.3 and 14.1 %, respectively, mainly due to FAs (Table 1). Identical genotypes for all three types of swabs were observed at only 12 of the 20 analysed individuals (60 %). Eight individuals exhibited divergent genotypes at one to seven loci for skin and/or cloaca swabs when compared to the corresponding buccal swab (Fig. 1). Our data set partly exhibited the consistency of FAs across skin and cloaca swabs at some loci (N=7), indicating that the high GERs of skin and cloaca swabs was not due to technical problems. The fact that skin and cloaca swabs did not show the same FAs at all instances might be due to the even lower DNA traces of the foreign individuals (e.g. sexual partner), which amplify inconsistently by chance. During the mating procedure, one or several males grasp the females with their forelegs, forming a big lump of frogs. Therefore, the external swabbing of amphibians during mating season, especially for explosive breeders like the common frog or the common toad, could result in high contamination rates. Consequently, skin and cloaca swabs should be applied outside the mating season only. However, this may increase the sampling effort compared to the high and centralised abundance at breeding ponds during the mating season. Cleaning the skin of frogs or toads with water before swabbing may improve the quality of swabs though, also for amphibians caught at fences in buckets. Nevertheless, for newts, e.g. those which are typically caught individually in bottles, skin and cloaca swabs might be feasible.
Beja-Pereira et al. ( 2009) reviewed that non-invasive genetic sampling is nowadays common in wildlife studies and that buccal, skin and cloaca swabs of amphibians and reptiles provide reliable DNA sources for microsatellite analyses. Prunier et al. (2012) also showed that skin swabs are a good alternative to buccal swabs especially for small and vulnerable amphibians. Also for reptiles, cloaca swabs are a reliable alternative to blood sampling and toe clipping (Miller 2006;Lanci et al. 2012). With this study, we agree that skin, but also cloaca, swabs are easier to conduct, come with a lower risk of injuries for the amphibians and produce comparably good-quality DNA for population genetic analyses. However, we showed that skin and cloaca swabs are not a reliable method of DNA sampling for all amphibian species regarding the respective collection practices. DNA contaminations could lead to distortion of genotyping results what eminently inhibits further analysis. To totally omit the possibility of contaminations with foreign individuals, we recommend that external swabbing should only be conducted if contact of individuals can be excluded.
